new_statements.rule_in_words: Yaweyuha is described as a register-tone language (two tones, H and L, one per syllable; Potts et al. 1974 tentatively add a rising tone on a few monosyllables), with very low functional load. The author states explicitly that word-stress patterns have not been analysed; no stress placement rule exists in any of the three SIL descriptions.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 3: in syllables containing two vowels the tone of the second vowel may differ from the first. Potts, James & Deibler 1974 (4.5): high tone has a down-glide allotone on the final syllable of final verbs; general downdrift over an utterance. OPD 1992: tone not written, very low functional load.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is assigned per syllable of the (phonological) word; the stress remark refers to 'phonological words'. No phrase-level prosody beyond downdrift is described.
new_statements.identity_note: All three sources describe Yaweyuha (also called Yabiyufa), ISO yby = Glottolog yawe1241; 1974 data from speakers of Apoeto village (Unggai census division, Goroka sub-district). The 1976 source is a Gahuku-Yaweyuha comparison; the quoted sentences refer to Yaweyuha specifically (tone statement covers both languages).

sources.citation: SIL. 1992 [printed 2004]. Organised Phonology Data: Yaweyuha (Yabiyufa) Language [YBY], Goroka, Eastern Highlands Province. Data checked by Ellis Deibler, September 1992. 4 pp.
sources.note: p.3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': 'Yaweyuha has two phonemic tones, each syllable carrying one of the tones' (nama LH 'bird' vs HH 'louse'; no H 'water' vs L 'you eat!'). Orthographic conventions: 'Tone is not written. It has a very low functional load.' Nothing said about stress.

sources.citation: Potts, Denise, Dorothy James & Ellis Deibler. 1974. Yaweyuha phonemes. Unpublished ms., SIL, Ukarumpa. 10 pp. (SIL PNG archive item 50162; scanned 2008)
sources.note: Phoneme chart (p.2) lists Tone: High, Low, Rising; sec. 3.3 (p.6) tone contrasts (high vs low, low vs rising, high vs rising); p.7 'There has not been time to do an analysis of the tone system of Yaweyuha, and the conclusions... are highly tentative'; 4.5 (p.8) high tone has a down-glide allotone on the final syllable of final verbs; downdrift. The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere; no stress statement.
